items.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
items.summary: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

items.body: Unfolding crisis shows importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds. He is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises. Continue reading...

items.body:

Senator Jacqui Lambie is responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament, at a rate of 406 swear words per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images

Potty-mouthed MPs ranked as Australian parliament sets new swearing record

One serial sweary offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’

• Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here

When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit” the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a new low” in federal politics.

Dick may have been on to something.

New analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.

Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006.

Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme.

Line chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament from 2006 to 2026. The rate fluctuates but trends upwards, rising from about 16 in 2006 to a peak of 37 in 2026, with a low of around 12 in 2009. A dotted trend line highlights the overall increase.

While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber.

So why bother?

Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be said for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June.

But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair.

“Debate is fierce and strong, and apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said.

“Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.”

And to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house.

An oral tradition

Described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by The Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly.

Excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary.

Swearing and swearing allegiance

Much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians.

Stacked bar chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, 2006–2026. Bill Heffernan leads with 877.2, followed by Jacqui Lambie (406.3), Derryn Hinch (398.4), Glenn Sterle (294.3), Russell Matheson (206.9), David Shoebridge (179.5), Pauline Hanson (169.5), Jordon Steele-John (167.9) and Steph Hodgins-May (161.6). Mild swear words make up most of each total, with smaller contributions from strong and extreme language. Only politicians who spoke more than 100,000 words are included.

Jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”.

“I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics.

“It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.”

Not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use”, or rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it.

However, when excluding these cases our analysis shows that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9, to 18.9 in 2022-5.

Line chart showing the three-year rolling rate of politicians’ own-use swearing per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, by party, from 2008 to 2026. One Nation peaks at about 175 in 2024 before falling to 110 in 2026. The Greens rise unevenly, reaching nearly 100 in 2026. Independents peak at about 80 in 2017 before declining sharply. Labor and Liberal rates remain below 15 throughout, while the Nationals reach about 24 in 2026.

Broken down by party, One Nation are the worst offenders, swearing for the sake of it at 7.4 times the rate of Labor – perhaps unsurprising, given that the party leader, Pauline Hanson, ranks fourth among discursively active politicians for use of foul language.

Dick said he had strived to improve the tone of discussion in parliament, believing that greater diversity in politics and in the chamber – with more women, more First Nations MPs and people from multicultural backgrounds – had also changed dynamics of debate.

Asked about recent heated moments in parliament, he said he recalled only two major moments in the lower house in recent years Hamilton’s June storm-out and fellow Liberal MP Dan Tehan’s demand to “cut the crap” in August.

“I want to ensure among our people and our democracy, that we fight hard to disagree more civilly … But I’m a big believer in upholding traditions and standards. When things get a bit heated, I’ll take firm action,” Dick said.

Notes on the analysis

Politicians’ speeches from both Houses of Parliament were analysed for the years 2006 to 2026. For each speech, the number of swearwords were counted using the these categories:

• Mild: bloody, damn, crap, bugger, bastard, bulldust, arse, mongrel, boofhead, bollocks

• Strong: prick, shit, bullshit, piss, piss off, dickhead, arsehole, shithouse, wanker

• Extreme: fucking, cunt, fuck, fuck off, fucker, fucked, motherfucker

To control for politicians’ tenure length and verbosity affecting swearing totals, swearing numbers were converted to a rate per million words by dividing the total swearwords by the total number of words spoken for that politician in that year, or for the total time period.

To separate swearing in a politician’s own voice from quotes, idioms and literal uses, an LLM was used to read the speech text surrounding each swearword and sort these into categories. A random sample of the results were manually checked, to achieve an agreement of 97% on whether a use was the speaker’s own. Therefore these figures are approximate.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network. Miley Cyrus weds drummer Maxx Morando in California – reports

Grammy-winning pop star and Morando reportedly tied the knot ⁠at a private ceremony in Palm ​Springs

Grammy-winning pop star Miley ⁠Cyrus married her longtime partner, drummer Maxx Morando, ⁠in California on ⁠Saturday, ​People magazine and other US entertainment news outlets ⁠reported.

Cyrus and Morando reportedly tied the knot ⁠at a private ceremony in Palm ​Springs, ‌a month ‌after performing Let’s Get Married together at ‌the Hollywood Bowl. The song appears on Cyrus’s latest studio album, Bass Persuades.

Representatives for both Cyrus and ‌Morando did not immediately respond to a Reuters’ request ​for comment.

Morando is the drummer for Liily, a Los Angeles-based alternative rock band ⁠affiliated with Atlantic Records, according to ​the ​band’s website.

The Flowers singer ​was previously married ​to Australian actor ‌Liam ​Hemsworth, ​who filed for divorce in Los Angeles in 2019.

Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war

UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

A vessel on fire in the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems

Read more

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

Pugh, 56, is a UN patron of the oceans. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

NFL’s Jaylen Harrell reportedly assaulted driver before crash that left player seriously injured

• Incident occurred in Tampa on Friday morning

• Crash leaves linebacker with serious injuries

Tampa police are investigating whether Tennessee Titans linebacker Jaylen Harrell assaulted a rideshare driver before a crash that left the NFL player in hospital.

The Tampa ⁠Police Department, in ⁠a preliminary report, said Harrell was in the back seat of the car around 8.45am on Friday in the backseat when “he reportedly assaulted the driver while ⁠the vehicle was in motion.” The driver then swerved, struck another car and collided ⁠with a utility pole, per the police report.

Harrell was thrown from the backseat, hit the windshield ‌and lost consciousness, according to ‌the police report. Harrell remains in hospital with serious injuries, while the rideshare ‌driver, a man in his 30s, sustained “minor injuries” and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the other vehicle, a woman in her 50s, was not injured, the police said.

The Titans issued a statement on Saturday ‌morning but did not disclose Harrell’s condition or the injuries he suffered, nor did they mention the assault accusation. The 24-year-old has not played this season after tearing an ACL in the preseason.

“We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information,” the team said ⁠in the statement. “At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an ‌update when appropriate.”

The accident occurred in Tampa, Harrell’s hometown.

Harrell played college football at Michigan before the Titans picked him in the seventh round of the 2024 draft. He played in every game in his first two seasons and recorded 4.5 sacks. His father, James, played eight seasons in the NFL before becoming a successful high school coach.

items.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
items.summary: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police…
items.body:
Alexander Lewis-Ranwell being released from a police station. Photograph: CPS/PA

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell being released from a police station. Photograph: CPS/PA

Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness. Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell. Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/PA

The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology. The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw. Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.

Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.

One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.

Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.

Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.

Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.

The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.

NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

A police spokesperson said the force was addressing “areas of learning” and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: “Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.”

The IOPC said the family had a right to ask for a review of the internal investigation and that it had not yet received a request.

Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad. For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler. Continue reading...

items.title: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
items.summary: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels • Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of th…
items.body:
The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ after two weeks of fierce negotiations

Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse

The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Darragh O’Brien (centre) and Wopke Hoekstra, the EU climate commissioner, speak outside a plenary session at Cop31 on Sunday. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations.

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

For many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis. Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, while African ministers made a dramatic intervention on Friday saying: “We did not come here to beg.”

Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, summed up the view of many on Friday when he said: “The Cop presidents want to tell us this has been a great Cop. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst Cop ever.”

On Sunday, he added: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create.... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

items.title: ‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post
items.summary: Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him UK politics live – latest updates Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin…
items.body:
Vladimir Putin, right, and the US president, Donald Trump, hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China last week. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

Vladimir Putin, right, and the US president, Donald Trump, hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China last week. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post

Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him

• UK politics live – latest updates

Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.”

The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

But the photo with Putin, showing Trump leaning towards the Russian leader to talk to him as they met at the summit, posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform overnight, prompted condemnation in the UK.

Asked for his reaction, Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, the British party most closely associated with Trump, replied: “Horror.”

He told Sky News: “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Asked whether Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, who is a friend of Trump, would speak to the US president about this, Tice replied: “Oh, there have been a number of occasions where one could agree with Trump, and then disagree with him.

“There have been more occasions recently when clearly we have disagreed with him and said so very explicitly. And in a sense, that’s the nature of long friendships. Sometimes you’ll agree and sometimes you’ll disagree. And, I think the disagreements are growing.”

Nigel Farage speaks during a Trump rally at Goodyear airport in Phoenix, Arizona in October 2020. Photograph: Rick D’Elia/EPA

Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices.

items.title: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week. The country has been g…
items.body:
Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal

Read more

The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.

“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.

President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

A student turns in her tablet and smartphone at a high school in Seoul ahead of the suneung exams. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.

Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

With Agence France-Presse

items.summary: Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns…
items.body:
The Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, which contains the UK’s largest telescope, is facing closure, with its UKRI funding withdrawn from March 2028. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

The Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, which contains the UK’s largest telescope, is facing closure, with its UKRI funding withdrawn from March 2028. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts

Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership

A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.

“Writing to a CEO in this tone and to this intent is an extraordinary step for this union to have to take,” Clancy wrote.

He warned: “Whilst there are legitimate cost pressures facing UKRI, ultimately any cuts will reduce the UK’s national science capability at a time when it is most needed.”

This year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), the government’s infrastructure funding agency, which is part of UKRI, revealed it needed to make £162m in savings by 2030.

While the core budget of the STFC remains broadly flat at about £835m a year, it is under financial pressure as a result of several factors. These include soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates. The last has resulted in an increase in costs relating to international facilities such as Cern.

The future of Jodrell Bank Observatory is at risk. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

As a result, in July UKRI released a plan to balance the STFC’s budget by 2030, revealing research projects and national facilities are to face significant changes.

“As responsible custodians of public funds, which I very much view our job is to be, we have to make sure that our costs are in line with our budget and that we don’t overspend the budget available to us,” Chapman said at the time, adding that it was important to prioritise spending in areas that made the biggest scientific impact.

World-class Jodrell Bank is under threat and UK risks a physics brain drain

Read more

The future of the UK’s largest telescope at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire has been put at risk, while the Diamond Light Source, the Central Laser Facility and the Isis Neutron and Muon Source, all in Oxfordshire, will remain operational but have been told to make efficiency savings.

The Clara facility in Cheshire – one of the world’s most advanced medium-energy electron beam facilities, which develops and tests next-generation accelerator technologies – is to be mothballed.

Clancy wrote in his letter to Chapman: “Our members working at UKRI do vital work which puts our country at the cutting edge of scientific developments and industrial applications and has considerable benefits across high-growth sectors, as well as in medical research and treatment. To pause or ‘mothball’ funding for many of the facilities where they work is to risk permanently losing the expertise that underpins the sector.”

The opening of a voluntary exit scheme to UKRI employees was also flagged by Clancy, who said the scheme was launched in parallel with the STFC cuts and without the requisite consultation on the organisational change plan with the recognised trade unions. His letter urges a pause to enable proper consultation and evidence-gathering on the cuts’ potential impact.

“In the absence of our requests leading to any productive engagement, we have lost confidence in your position as CEO,” Clancy wrote to Chapman.

The Diamond Light Source, at the Harwell science and innovation campus in Oxfordshire, produces intense beams of light for scientific research. It has been told to make efficiency savings. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

Prof Leszek Borysiewicz, the chair of UKRI, said the board had full confidence in Chapman and his leadership team.

“We support the direction of the ambitious reform programme UKRI is undertaking to become more effective, agile and better able to respond to the country’s priorities and needs,” Borysiewicz said. “Delivering transformation on this scale is a substantial undertaking involving difficult decisions about how UKRI operates, where resources are focused and how we deliver the greatest impact.

“UKRI has been clear with staff and unions about the direction of change, including its new mission and funding model, greater join-up across programmes and the unification of professional services. The decisions announced this year followed extensive engagement with staff, research and user communities, alongside detailed consideration of the impacts of different funding choices.”

The science minister, Chris McDonald, said: “I have full confidence in Ian Chapman’s leadership of UKRI. The organisation’s ongoing and essential transformation programme will ensure projects supported through our record £86bn commitment to R&D will deliver maximum impact and value for money – as the British public rightly expect.

“I know from personal experience that this transformation will have a significant and personal impact on workers and others affected, and we will continue to engage the UKRI workforce. I am committed to working closely with UKRI, the workers, and their trade unions as we continue to progress the transformation plan.”

The date mirrors the city’s 901 area code, and gives residents a reason to come together to celebrate the city and the people who love it. When 9/01 Day falls on a weekday, as it did this year, the celebration starts the weekend prior, extending the festivities. Groups across the city hosted celebrations featuring food vendors, DJs, musicians and members of the Memphis Grizzlies , the local NBA team, while dozens of local businesses offered $9.01-themed specials. But for the families of 121 people, this past 1 September will be remembered for a different reason – just days prior, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained their friends and relatives, conducting one of the largest single-day raids in the country this year, and the largest known one in Memphis . items.summary: Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned. Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Gol…
items.body:
A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines they did not accept responsibility for. Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty Images

A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines they did not accept responsibility for. Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty Images

Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool

Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

Criminals are using cloned plates to evade detection and avoid paying penalties for dangerous or illegal driving.

A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for: most of which are believed to be a result of cloning. The number of complaints was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the number recorded in 2018.

To help victims, a new reporting tool has been launched in England and Wales. The tool is designed to make it easier to alert the authorities by allowing victims to report a cloned plate directly to the police online who will also inform the DVLA. There is a new section on the government’s website that explains how to appeal incorrect fines or charges.

The government has also issued consumer guidance on how to avoid falling foul of driving with an illegal number plate after it emerged that a third of motorists stopped in number plate operations this year had no idea they had one.

Unreal deals: the scam websites targeting Black Friday bargain hunters

Read more

Early findings from the police suggest that, in addition to deliberate criminal use, the public are unwittingly being sold incorrect plates. Stolen secondhand cars can be fitted with cloned plates and the government advises that you check the car’s registration number is consistent with information held by the DVLA.

The roads minister, Justin Madders, said: “Illegal plates are being used by criminals, but it is also the case that innocent motorists can have illegal plates on their vehicles without their knowledge.

“We are going to make it easier for victims of cloned plates to report them as well as [launching] webpages to help drivers when they buy number plates and used cars from reputable sellers. These are small everyday fixes from the government which could help you avoid unwelcome attention from police.”

It took Yarwood months to sort out the mess left by the criminals who racked up the fines in six days.

“I never paid any of them … but the difficulty contesting them is gobsmacking,” she said. “You have to prove your innocence and the fact that I was not in the country was not enough.”

She said after she had reported the cloned plates her husband was stopped while driving the car. “But not in an unpleasant way,” she added. “It was fine.”

If it happens again, Yarwood has been advised to change her registration which she says is a “whole thing I didn’t want to have to do. So I’m waiting. I hope they don’t.”

Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’

Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.

However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.

“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy

While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.

“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.

Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.

The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.

“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

items.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
items.body:
Figure caption,

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam

ByJaroslav Lukiv

South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

items.summary: Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.…
items.body:
Indian Youth Congress members protest outside a Meta office building in Mumbai, India. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Indian Youth Congress members protest outside a Meta office building in Mumbai, India. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes

Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.

The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

‘Humanity is a privilege’: Umar Khalid on his six years in an Indian jail without trial

Read more

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.

India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

Congress members burn signs during a protest in Mumbai. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety ⁠or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.

A video ‌from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.

In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.

An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it ​had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

Police clash with Youth Congress members at a protest in Hyderabad. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.

“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Reporters Without Borders has ​said the removal of journalistic content from social media ​has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media ​companies hardly any time to review ‌and decide on takedown requests.

In ​February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies ​to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.

Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.

“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

items.summary: New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people • Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profite…
items.body:
Copper works in the lower Swansea valley, Charles Pascoe Grenfell and El Cobre mine, Cuba. Cobre was ‘likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere’ by the 1840s. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy

Copper works in the lower Swansea valley, Charles Pascoe Grenfell and El Cobre mine, Cuba. Cobre was ‘likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere’ by the 1840s. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy

Highly lucrative: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba

New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

In the 1840s, Cuba was the most important foreign source of copper ore for the UK. Copper was critical to Manchester’s cotton industry, railways and telegraphy.

Previous research has revealed that dozens of financiers involved in the founding in 1694 of the Bank of England invested in enslavement.

Now, Evans’s research reveals that ties between key figures in the UK’s financial system and enslavement of African peoples continued even after the government outlawed it.

Britain abolished its trade in enslaved people in 1807 and passed legislation abolishing slavery in most of its empire in 1833.

However, as Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act was coming into force, “City of London figures” were developing mining of El Cobre’s copper ore deposits, an operation which depended on enslavement in Spanish-controlled Cuba.

Key players in the highly lucrative operation included the Bank of England directors Charles Pascoe Grenfell (1790-1867) and William Thompson (1792-1854), acting in a private capacity.

Enslaved copper miners at El Cobre were likely to have been trafficked to Cuba by illegal voyages from the Bight of Biafra, in modern-day Nigeria, as Evans details in his book, Slavery’s Long Goodbye – Capitalism, Nationalism and Christianity in the Age of British Emancipation.

The death rate at El Cobre means it is likely that thousands of Africans were exploited there. Their life stories remain largely undocumented. At the time, slavery was legal in Cuba but the importation of enslaved people was not.

As a partner in the Cobre mining and export company, Grenfell was a driving force in enslaved miners’ exploitation.

Cobre was “likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere” by the 1840s, Evans said. Investors who held Cobre shares from the outset received £102 in dividends for every £40 share between 1836 and 1865.

Enslavement at El Cobre ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. Illustration: Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

Grenfell was also a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from the mine, in an era when the Welsh port was the centre of the global copper trade.

Meanwhile, Thompson, a former lord mayor of London, exploited enslaved miners through the ore export firm he directed, the Royal Santiago Company.

The UK is facing increased pressure to make a formal apology to Caribbean and African nations for Britain’s centuries-long perpetuation of transatlantic chattel slavery. Commonwealth leaders say “structured dialogue” with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin in the next year.

While the Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has claimed Britain has nothing to apologise for, scholarship – dating back to the Trinidadian statesman Eric Williams’s 1944 book, Capitalism and Slavery – reveals the global impact of the colonialism and chattel enslavement that was integral to British capitalism’s success.

Evans, a former professor at the University of South Wales, said: “As Britain ostentatiously winds down its own slave system in the 1830s, British capital is boosting slavery elsewhere in the western hemisphere.

“The illegal trade, involving French and Spanish merchants, was flourishing and substantial. There were British (anti-slavery) patrols off the coast of Cuba, but they’re relatively few in number and intercept only a very small proportion of slave ships.”

Conditions at El Cobre were “extremely brutal”, with daily violence and torture. “Slave catchers” were employed to snatch miners who tried to escape to the mountains.

after newsletter promotion

In 1817, under British pressure, Spanish authorities signed a treaty that banned trafficking enslaved Africans to Cuba. But as Cuba’s sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved African workers, local colonial authorities ignored it, with 25,000 captives arriving in 1859 alone.

Charles Grenfell was a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from Cuba. Illustration: Digitised by Bethan Jones/Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

In 1843, pressure from the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society prompted legislation intended to prohibit British subjects from owning enslaved people in other jurisdictions, after undercover investigations exposed British mining companies’ activities in Brazil and Cuba, including at El Cobre.

But after lobbying by mining interests, parliament diluted the legislation, allowing companies to retain enslaved workers as their “property” and hire others. The concessions prompted abolitionists to withdraw their support for the law, which failed to end the exploitation.

Neither Grenfell nor Thompson appears to have faced legal penalties for their involvement. Grenfell became the Liberal MP for Preston in the late 1840s, later boasting that his father had been an abolitionist. Grenfell remained a B of E director until 1864.

Enslavement at El Cobre finally ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. The rebel commander proclaimed the miners’ emancipation on New Year’s Eve, and formerly enslaved workers later joined Cuba’s liberation army.

Evans’s book explores Britain’s overlapping histories of slavery, capitalism and missionary Christianity through the lives of Grenfell and two of his cousins.

Evans added: “The British in the early 19th century had started to understand slavery as a national sin.

“In the classical age of abolition, you could do things like abstain from eating sugar from the West Indies.

“But with copper, you can’t do that because it’s embodied in the industrial world, and, in the age of joint-stock capitalism, you have many British people who invest in mining companies who genuinely didn’t know these companies were using enslaved workers.

“Slavery was rendered invisible by the complexity of industrial society. But British engagement with slavery continued long after Emancipation. It involved the mercantile-financial elite of London as well as hundreds, possibly thousands, of rank-and-file investors from the Victorian middle class.”

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “We have previously acknowledged the role of former governors and directors in the slave trade.”

items.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
items.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByJessica Lamb

Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

Image source, Reuters

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external

"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.

"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.

The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."

The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.

Image source, FilmMagic via Getty Images

Image caption,

Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.

In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.

In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

items.title: Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing
items.summary: Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says. Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroye…
items.body:
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, about 50km from Jakarta, caught fire on Saturday afternoon. Photograph: Mohammad Hashemi Rafsanjani/AFP/Getty Images

The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, about 50km from Jakarta, caught fire on Saturday afternoon. Photograph: Mohammad Hashemi Rafsanjani/AFP/Getty Images

Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing

Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones

A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

A drone view of emergency crews gathered outside the factory in Indonesia’s Banten province. Photograph: Reuters

The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.

“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.

Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.

Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

Smoke rises from the factory on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters

“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.

The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

Crews from Indonesia’s Basarnas search and rescue agency inspect the site. Photograph: BASARNAS/AP

Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.

In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.

In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.
